ethiopia.title: PM Abiy's Medemer Govt Senior Leadership Taking 'Military Training'at Hurso Center
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy's Medemer Govt Senior Leadership Taking 'Military Training'at Hurso Center - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy's Medemer Govt Senior Leadership Taking 'Military Training'at Hurso Center Addis Standard PM Abiy said that military science and experience could help cultivate the “discipline, accountability, coordination, and sense of patriotism” expected of government leaders. 31 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Senior leaders of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's Medemer Government are undergoing military training at the Hurso Military Training Center, according to PM Abiy, who said the exercise as part of efforts to strengthen leadership capacity, discipline, national security, and the implementation of its broader development vision. In a statement outlining the rationale for the training, Abiy said the Medemer Government's ambition to "build Ethiopia's civilization" based on comprehensive prosperity required leaders who were physically developed, morally strong, intellectually prepared, and mature in wisdom. "Leadership requires comprehensive preparedness," Abiy said, describing comprehensive prosperity as encompassing material and spiritual well-being alongside cultural and moral development. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines He argued that military science and experience could help cultivate the "discipline, accountability, coordination, and sense of patriotism" expected of government leaders. According to Abiy, the training is intended to equip senior officials with skills and experience that can be applied to implementing the government's Medemer vision, including aligning strategic thinking, mobilizing public participation, fulfilling commitments to citizens, and strengthening national security. The prime minister said military training could also help leaders improve coordination across government structures, from the grassroots to the national level, while fostering a sense of responsibility for the country's future. "Military science, experience, and life are unrivaled in shaping human purpose and personality," Abiy said, arguing that military institutions instill physical and moral discipline, work ethic, teamwork, and readiness to carry out assigned responsibilities. He further linked the exercise to the government's ambition to build what he described as an "unshakeable country" capable of resisting internal and external challenges, while preparing succeeding generations for leadership. "Soldiers have targets; civilians have a purpose. The goal of both is to achieve victory," Abiy said. "By harmonizing both disciplines, we will create a generation that both hits the target and achieves the purpose." The statement from the Prime Minister not specify the number of government officials participating in the training, its duration, or the full range of activities included in the program. ethiopia.summary: Senior leaders of Ethiopia's Medemer Government, under Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, are currently undergoing military training at the Hurso Military Training Center. Abiy emphasized that this initiative aims to enhance leadership capacity, discipline, and national security, aligning with the government's broader development vision. He stated that military science and experience could foster essential qualities such as accountability, coordination, and patriotism among government officials. The training is designed to prepare leaders physically, morally, and intellectually for their responsibilities, contributing to the government's goal of building a prosperous and resilient Ethiopia. Abiy highlighted the importance of harmonizing military discipline with civilian purpose to create a generation capable of achieving both targets and broader societal goals. However, details regarding the number of participants, the duration of the training, and specific activities involved have not been disclosed. This initiative reflects the government's commitment to strengthening leadership and ensuring a secure future for the nation.

ethiopia.content: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 2, 2026 - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: All of Africa Today - November 2, 2026 AllAfrica AllAfrica logo 2 November 2026 allAfrica.com By Melody Chironda Sudan's El Fasher Remains a Ghost Town One Year After RSF Takeover One year after the capture of El Fasher, North Darfur, by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the city remains largely deserted, with survivors and aid workers reporting widespread destruction, fear, and ongoing human rights abuses. Thousands of residents are still missing, and others are believed to be detained in overcrowded prisons where torture, disease and inhumane conditions have been reported. 40,000 to 60,000 people are estimated to have returned or visited the city. Many are still reluctant to return because of the trauma, the insecurity, and the fear that new arrivals have taken their homes. International investigators have documented mass killings and sexual violence during the siege. The UN estimates that around 6,000 people were killed. However, researchers believe the actual death toll could be significantly higher. HRW Accuses Zambian Forces of Abductions, Torture and Crackdown on Critics Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Human Rights Watch has accused Zambian security forces of forcibly disappearing, arbitrarily detaining and abusing opposition members, journalists, lawyers and government critics following the August 2026 general elections. The organisation documented 14 apparent cases of enforced disappearances, 61 cases of alleged abuse in custody and 71 cases of potentially politically motivated arrests or prolonged detention without charge. Several detainees have reportedly faced beatings, torture, restricted access to lawyers and medical care, while opposition figures, including leader Brian Mundubile, have been charged with treason. Human Rights Watch has called on President Hakainde Hichilema's government to end the crackdown, release those arbitrarily detained and investigate alleged abuses, including the controversial killing of former government minister Mutotwe Kafwaya during a security raid. Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed Sends Cabinet Ministers for Military Training Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put cabinet ministers and senior government officials through military training . He said that military discipline can help strengthen leadership and advance national development. Images shared on social media show ministers, including Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba, participating in exercises at the Hurso military training centre. Abiy said that military institutions can teach discipline, patriotism, teamwork and accountability, helping create leaders capable of achieving the country's development ambitions. The unusual initiative comes as Ethiopia faces ongoing conflicts in Tigray, Amhara and Oromia, as well as heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea. Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions. Gauteng Shuts 20 Liquor Outlets in GBV Crackdown Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi said that the province has shut down 20 liquor outlets following more than 7,300 inspections as part of efforts to tackle gender-based violence and protect women and children. The province plans to deploy 1,022 response teams across 122 high-risk areas and recruit an additional 56 social workers to support victims and survivors. Authorities are also strengthening specialised sexual offences courts, victim-friendly facilities, shelters and security measures, while municipalities work to address crime hotspots. However, Lesufi acknowledged that progress remains slow, with only 21 of the 67 government instructions to combat violence against women and children completed. 38 remain underway and eight have yet to begin. DR Congo Hunger Crisis to Worsen, With 30 Million at Risk More than 28.8 million people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo are expected to face acute food insecurity through December, according to the latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) assessment. The crisis is being driven by ongoing conflict and displacement in the east, rising food and fuel prices, disease outbreaks, including the expanding Ebola epidemic, and climate-related shocks. North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri remain the worst-affected provinces, with more than 10 million people experiencing high levels of food insecurity. The situation is expected to worsen between January and June 2027 when the number of people facing acute hunger could reach 30.3 million, including 4.2 million in emergency conditions. Malawi's President Says He Remained in Control During South Africa Stay Malawi President Peter Mutharika has assured citizens that he remained in full control of government during his three-week private leave in South Africa, maintaining regular contact with ministers, government officials and his party. Mutharika dismissed concerns about his absence. He said that the country remained under control and that any challenges were largely political. His return comes as Malawi faces foreign currency shortages, a fuel crisis and frequent power cuts. His absence also sparked speculation about his health on social media, although he did not directly address the rumours. He called for national unity and urged Malawians to work together for the country's progress. ethiopia.title: Diplomatic Visibility, Strategic Deterrence and Growing Stakes in the Red Sea Region
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Diplomatic Visibility, Strategic Deterrence and Growing Stakes in the Red Sea Region - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Diplomatic Visibility, Strategic Deterrence and Growing Stakes in the Red Sea Region 1 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) The final week of October 2026 brought Ethiopia into sharper international focus, as the country advanced its defence modernization, strengthened strategic partnerships and renewed attention to its interests in the Abay (Nile) Basin and Red Sea region. From the announcement of the delivery of advanced fighter jets and plans to acquire sophisticated air defence systems to high-level diplomatic engagements at the Russia-Africa Summit, Ethiopia's activities reflected the growing intersection of national security, economic ambitions and regional geopolitics. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's participation in the Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow provided an important platform for advancing bilateral and continental cooperation. His announcement that Ethiopia had received its first 12 Su-35 fighter jets and was set to acquire four batteries of S-400 air defence systems also brought the country's military modernization into the international spotlight. Meanwhile, the Third Ethiopian Water and Energy Week highlighted the country's efforts to strengthen water-resource management amid rising demand from agriculture, industry and a growing population. In Addis Ababa, the introduction of the first 26 natural gas-powered city buses marked another step towards reducing fuel imports, lowering transport costs and expanding the use of locally sourced energy. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Beyond these developments, discussions surrounding Ethiopia's interests in the Abay River and sustainable access to the Red Sea continued to feature prominently in national and international discourse. Together, these developments underscored Ethiopia's efforts to strengthen its national capabilities, diversify international partnerships and advance its economic and strategic interests in an increasingly interconnected regional environment. Defence Modernization: Ethiopia Advances Strategic Deterrence One of the week's most consequential announcements came from Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who disclosed that Ethiopia had taken delivery of its first 12 Russian-made Su-35 4++ generation fighter jets and was preparing to receive four batteries of S-400 air defence systems. The Prime Minister described the development as a significant milestone in the country's efforts to strengthen national defence and security capabilities, emphasizing the importance of building military readiness during peacetime to deter potential threats. "Today, in accordance with our prior agreement with the Russian government, we have taken delivery of the first twelve Su-35 4++ Generation fighter jets," he announced. He further disclosed that Ethiopia would receive four batteries of S-400 air defence systems, marking another major component of the country's military modernization programme. The Prime Minister elaborated that the delivery was expedited ahead of schedule following high-level engagements with the Russian government, including discussions with President Vladimir Putin. Highlighting the capabilities of the newly acquired aircraft, Abiy said the Su-35 combines advanced radar technology, high manoeuvrability and air-to-air and air-to-ground combat capabilities. He also pointed to its ability to detect and engage aerial threats, including cruise missiles and certain ballistic targets. The acquisition signals Ethiopia's intention to strengthen its air capabilities as part of a broader effort to modernize the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF). Beyond acquiring sophisticated military platforms, the country's evolving defence priorities also place emphasis on operational readiness, technological capabilities and the institutional capacity required to maintain and sustain modern military systems. The announcement has consequently drawn international attention to Ethiopia's changing defence posture and its implications for the wider Horn of Africa and Red Sea security environment. Russia-Africa Summit: Advancing Ethiopia's Strategic Partnerships Ethiopia's defence announcement coincided with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's participation in the Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, where he engaged in bilateral and multilateral discussions aimed at expanding cooperation across strategic sectors. Among the key engagements was his meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, during which the two leaders discussed ways to deepen the longstanding relationship between their countries. PM Abiy pointed out that the discussions explored opportunities for expanding cooperation in nuclear energy, healthcare, trade and other areas of mutual interest. The meeting reflected the two countries' continued interest in broadening their partnership beyond traditional diplomatic relations into sectors central to Ethiopia's long-term economic and technological ambitions. In a gesture underscoring the importance of intellectual exchange and mutual understanding, the Ethiopian Prime Minister also presented Putin with the Russian edition of his book, Medemer . PM Abiy described the presentation as reflecting the shared commitment of the two countries to dialogue, mutual understanding and the continued advancement of bilateral relations. Addressing the summit, the Prime Minister emphasized the importance of translating longstanding diplomatic relationships and strategic commitments into tangible development outcomes. He identified food security and agricultural productivity, reliable energy supply, and skills and knowledge transfer as three essential pillars underpinning Ethiopia's development ambitions. He further noted that Ethiopia and Russia have maintained diplomatic relations for more than a century, founded on mutual respect and shared interests. As part of efforts to expand this historic partnership, the two countries are pursuing cooperation on the development of a nuclear power plant in Ethiopia, an initiative expected to contribute to the country's long-term energy ambitions. Prime Minister Abiy said the strategic partnership with Russia could help diversify Ethiopia's energy options, accelerate its development aspirations and strengthen cooperation in areas critical to national prosperity. Water and Energy: Strengthening the Foundation for Sustainable Development While defence and diplomacy attracted considerable international attention, Ethiopia's water and energy agenda remained another important focus during the week. The Third Ethiopian Water and Energy Week brought together policymakers, technical experts and other stakeholders to examine the country's progress and challenges in managing its water resources and expanding access to essential services. The third day of the event was dedicated to Water Day under the theme "Evidence to Action: Science-Based Solutions for Integrated WASH and Water Resource Management." Discussions focused on strengthening the identification, documentation and sustainable management of Ethiopia's surface and groundwater resources as population growth, industrialization and agricultural expansion continue to increase national demand. The gathering also provided an opportunity to assess progress over the past decade in drinking water supply and sanitation, recognize achievements and identify remaining gaps. For Ethiopia, effective water-resource management is closely linked to food security, energy generation, industrial development and public health. With agriculture remaining central to the national economy, improved water management and expanded irrigation infrastructure are increasingly important to strengthening agricultural productivity and reducing vulnerability to climate-related shocks. The discussions therefore highlighted the importance of translating scientific evidence, research and policy commitments into practical solutions that can support the country's long-term development. Addis Ababa Introduces Its First Natural Gas-Powered City Buses Another notable development during the week was the introduction of the first 26 natural gas-powered city buses into Addis Ababa's public transportation system. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced that the buses, converted from conventional fuel to natural gas, had officially entered service, marking a new phase in the capital's efforts to modernize public transport and diversify its energy sources. The initiative is expected to reduce the country's fuel import bill, lower public transport operating expenses and make transportation more affordable for passengers. the Prime Minister revealed that the transition is projected to cut passenger fares by half while reducing foreign currency expenditure on conventional fuels. He explained that the initiative followed months of work to transport domestically produced natural gas to Addis Ababa, establish refuelling facilities and retrofit existing buses. Beyond its immediate transport benefits, the project demonstrates efforts to expand the domestic application of locally available energy resources and strengthen technological and industrial capabilities. The Premier also disclosed that an additional 400 natural gas-powered buses were expected to arrive soon, as the government seeks to accelerate the transition towards more affordable and diversified public transportation. The initiative forms part of broader efforts to improve urban mobility, reduce dependence on imported petroleum products and deliver tangible economic benefits to citizens. Abay and Red Sea: Ethiopia's Strategic Interests Gain International Attention Alongside developments in defence, diplomacy and economic transformation, Ethiopia's interests in the Abay River and sustainable access to the Red Sea continued to attract attention from political leaders, analysts and international commentators. The country's geographical position, population size, economic ambitions and growing regional responsibilities have increasingly brought these issues into discussions about the future of the Horn of Africa. Former Prime Minister Hailemariam Desalegn described Ethiopia's pursuit of sustainable sea access as a legitimate national aspiration that should be addressed through dialogue, negotiations and mutually beneficial arrangements. He argued that the central question should not be whether Ethiopia needs access to the sea, but how such access can be secured peacefully while respecting the interests of all parties. With a population of approximately 130 million, a growing economy and a vast geographical area, Ethiopia is the world's most populous landlocked country. Hailemariam described the loss of direct maritime access as a historical development that continues to influence the country's economic and strategic interests. He also traced the region's present geographical arrangements to the European scramble for Africa in the 1880s, arguing that the issue deserves serious consideration rather than being passed on to future generations. His remarks added to the growing discussion about Ethiopia's maritime interests and the importance of pursuing regional solutions through constructive engagement. Meanwhile, former African Union Commission Chairperson Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma highlighted Ethiopia's broader continental significance, particularly its homegrown development approach and investments in energy. Speaking to ENA in Moscow ahead of the Russia-Africa Summit, Dlamini-Zuma described Ethiopia as an important model of African development and self-determination. Having led the African Union Commission from its headquarters in Addis Ababa between 2012 and 2017, she emphasized the country's unique responsibility as the diplomatic capital of Africa. She said Ethiopia should continue contributing to the vision of an integrated, peaceful and prosperous continent, driven by African leadership and the aspirations of its people. Her remarks highlighted the importance of Ethiopia's development experience and its role in advancing continental cooperation. A Week Reflecting Ethiopia's Expanding Strategic Priorities Taken together, the developments of the final week of October reflected several interconnected dimensions of Ethiopia's national priorities. The defence acquisitions highlighted efforts to strengthen military readiness and strategic deterrence. The Russia-Africa Summit provided an opportunity to expand international partnerships in energy, trade, healthcare and technology. The Water and Energy Week reinforced the importance of sustainable resource management, while the introduction of natural gas-powered buses demonstrated the practical application of domestic energy resources. At the same time, discussions surrounding the Abay River and Red Sea access underscored the enduring importance of geography, economic interests and regional cooperation in shaping Ethiopia's strategic outlook. These developments point to a broader national agenda in which security, economic transformation, technological advancement and diplomatic engagement increasingly intersect. As Ethiopia continues to pursue its development ambitions and navigate a changing regional and international environment, the challenge will be to translate these strategic priorities into sustainable economic gains, stronger national institutions and peaceful, mutually beneficial regional partnerships. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced the delivery of 12 Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets and plans to acquire S-400 air defense systems, emphasizing the importance of military readiness for national security. His participation in the Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow facilitated discussions on expanding cooperation in various sectors, including nuclear energy and trade. Concurrently, the Third Ethiopian Water and Energy Week focused on sustainable water resource management amid rising demands. Additionally, Addis Ababa introduced its first natural gas-powered city buses, aimed at reducing fuel imports and transportation costs. Discussions surrounding Ethiopia's need for sustainable access to the Red Sea highlighted its geopolitical aspirations, with calls for dialogue to address these interests peacefully. Overall, these developments reflect Ethiopia's commitment to enhancing its national capabilities and regional influence.

ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Abiy Joins Ministers in Military Drills, Calls for Disciplined Leadership - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Abiy Joins Ministers in Military Drills, Calls for Disciplined Leadership Addis Standard PM Abiy said that military science and experience could help cultivate the “discipline, accountability, coordination, and sense of patriotism” expected of government leaders. 1 November 2026 Horn Diplomat (Hargeisa) By Kadir Moustapha Addis Ababa — Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has joined ministers and senior government officials in military training, saying discipline and preparedness could strengthen civilian leadership and help deliver the government's development goals. Abiy participated in exercises at the Hurso military training centre on October 31. Photographs shared on his X account showed him seated outdoors with officials wearing beige training clothes. Participants included House of Federation Speaker Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba. "The government's leadership is engaged in intense military training," Abiy wrote in an October 31 post on X, according to an English translation of his Amharic-language statement. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn He said Ethiopia's ambitions required leaders who combined physical fitness with knowledge, ethical conduct and a commitment to public service. "It must be physically strong, morally steadfast, knowledgeable, and disciplined in conduct," he wrote, describing the leadership needed to advance those objectives. Abiy said military experience offered lessons in teamwork, accountability, readiness and coordination across different levels of government. Civilian officials could apply those principles to carrying out public duties and translating national priorities into practical results, he said. He linked the training to the government's broader strategy, including aligning administrative structures with national objectives, fulfilling commitments to citizens and safeguarding national security. The prime minister also argued that development should encompass material prosperity alongside spiritual, cultural and moral progress. Drawing a comparison between soldiers and civilian officials, Abiy said both needed discipline to accomplish their respective responsibilities. Combining lessons from military and civilian leadership could help develop leaders capable of achieving wider national goals, he said. His statement did not specify when the training programme began or how long it would continue. (Reporting by HornDiplomat News Desk) Read the original article on Horn Diplomat . ethiopia.title: U.S. Customs Releases Ethiopia-Made Solar Cell Shipments After Supply Chain Review
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: U.S. Customs Releases Ethiopia-Made Solar Cell Shipments After Supply Chain Review - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: U.S. Customs Releases Ethiopia-Made Solar Cell Shipments After Supply Chain Review 30 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has released shipments of solar cells manufactured at a Japanese company's facility in Ethiopia following a review of its supply chain documentation, SolarQuarter reported. TOYO Co., Ltd., a Japan-headquartered solar manufacturing company, announced on 29 October that CBP had completed its review after the company submitted documentation demonstrating the traceability of its supply chain, including the origins of polysilicon and wafers used in manufacturing the solar cells. The company said it cooperated with US authorities throughout the review process and provided detailed documentation on the sourcing of its production materials. The release of the shipments comes as TOYO seeks to expand its international manufacturing operations and strengthen its presence in the US market. The company operates a manufacturing facility in Humble, Texas, and is pursuing certification under CBP's Customs Trade Partnership Against Terrorism (CTPAT) programme, which is designed to strengthen supply chain security and import compliance. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn TOYO Chief Executive Officer Takahiko Onozuka welcomed the completion of the review, expressing appreciation for what he described as CBP's professional approach. He said the company remained committed to transparency and regulatory compliance as it expands its US operations. Onozuka also stressed the importance of providing customers with confidence in the origins of solar products through greater supply chain traceability. The development highlights the importance of supply chain documentation and regulatory compliance for solar manufacturers operating across multiple countries, particularly as scrutiny of the origins of imported products increases. The release of the shipments follows an ongoing US investigation into whether solar cell manufacturers operating in Ethiopia are circumventing existing American trade duties on Chinese solar products. In July 2026, Addis Standard reported that the US Department of Commerce had launched a country-wide investigation into imports of silicon solar cells from Ethiopia to determine whether they were circumventing longstanding antidumping and countervailing duty (AD/CVD) orders on Chinese solar products. The investigation followed a petition filed in May 2026 by eight US solar manufacturers -- DYCM Power, First Solar, Qcells, Silfab, Solx, Suniva, Swift Solar and Talon PV -- alleging that two manufacturers operating in Ethiopia, TOYO and Origin Solar, were using Chinese-origin wafers to produce solar cells in Ethiopia before assembling them into solar modules locally or in Vietnam for export to the US. According to the petition, nearly 70% of finished solar modules exported from Ethiopia contained Chinese components and underwent processing allegedly covered by existing US trade restrictions. Solar Power World reported that imports of Ethiopia-origin solar cells and modules, which were virtually nonexistent before July 2025, reached an estimated $277 million in the second half of that year, with shipments continuing to increase in 2026. The petitioners argued that the surge in exports coincided with increased shipments of key solar manufacturing inputs from China to Ethiopia. Both TOYO and Origin Solar subsequently submitted factual information to the Department of Commerce in response to the allegations. The investigation is expected to reach a preliminary determination by 10 December 2026, with a final decision anticipated around 10 May 2027. In the meantime, US Customs and Border Protection was instructed to suspend liquidation of relevant imports and apply cash deposit requirements pending the outcome. Any duties imposed could be applied retroactively to the investigation's initiation date. ethiopia.title: 'Ethiopia's Return to a Sea Port Is Inevitable': Navy Commander Calls for Regional Maritime Cooperation
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: 'Ethiopia's Return to a Sea Port Is Inevitable': Navy Commander Calls for Regional Maritime Cooperation - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: 'Ethiopia's Return to a Sea Port Is Inevitable': Navy Commander Calls for Regional Maritime Cooperation 30 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Ethiopian Navy Commander Vice Admiral Kindu Gezu has called for closer regional cooperation and dialogue on maritime security, saying Ethiopia's return to a seaport is inevitable and requires stronger engagement with neighboring countries. "Since Ethiopia's return to a sea port is inevitable, working closely and through dialogue with regional countries is essential," Kindu said on Friday, a day after the conclusion of a regional maritime security forum organized by the Ethiopian Navy Headquarters, according to the army. The forum brought together naval commanders and representatives from Yemen, Oman, Djibouti, Somaliland, and Puntland to exchange experiences and explore joint approaches to maritime search and rescue operations and regional security challenges. ENDF said the forum was organized with the support of the European Union. Kindu described the gathering as "the first of its kind in Ethiopia" to discuss regional maritime search and rescue plans, saying it demonstrated the Ethiopian Navy's growing capabilities and readiness to engage in regional and continental maritime affairs. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn He also highlighted growing security challenges around the Strait of Hormuz, warning that threats in the area could increasingly affect the wider region. No country, regardless of its strength, could independently ensure maritime security or resolve emerging challenges, he said, emphasizing the need for countries of different sizes to pool their capabilities. "The participating countries of the forum must work together to solve the problems observed in the region," Kindu said, adding that regional cooperation was essential to addressing maritime threats and ensuring safe maritime movement. Ethiopian Navy Deputy Commander for Operations Commodore Jemal Tufisa said the forum had helped establish practical foundations for regional cooperation through cross-border information sharing, identifying areas of concern, and conducting joint operational exercises. "We trust that upon returning to your respective countries, you will translate the lessons gained from the workshop into action, working effectively on regional maritime security and performing tasks with international acceptance," Jemal said. Rear Admiral Kenneth Nyagah, a search and rescue project expert, and Master Kuraja Mishini, manager of the Djibouti Code of Conduct, commended the Ethiopian Navy's initiative in creating communication channels for information sharing, coordinated decision-making, and joint responses to regional threats. Both expressed their commitment to continued cooperation. ethiopia.title: Fading Hopes, Rising Needs - Renewed Fighting Threatens Another Humanitarian Catastrophe in Tigray
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Fading Hopes, Rising Needs - Renewed Fighting Threatens Another Humanitarian Catastrophe in Tigray - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Fading Hopes, Rising Needs - Renewed Fighting Threatens Another Humanitarian Catastrophe in Tigray 30 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Renewed fighting in Tigray, northern Ethiopia, is pushing an already vulnerable population towards another humanitarian catastrophe. Nearly four years after the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement was signed to end the devastating war between the Ethiopian federal government and Tigrayan forces, renewed hostilities have raised serious concerns about civilian safety, mass displacement, food insecurity, and the disruption of essential services. For millions of people in Tigray, the consequences of the previous war have never truly ended. Families continue to struggle with displacement, hunger, damaged health facilities, destroyed livelihoods, and the loss of loved ones. The renewed violence threatens to reverse the limited progress made towards recovery and deepen the suffering of communities that have endured years of conflict. The severity of the crisis is evident not only in reports of casualties, growing humanitarian needs, and continuing displacement, but also in the experiences of people struggling to survive in displacement centers. Their testimonies reveal the human consequences of a crisis that extends far beyond the battlefield. This is not simply another security crisis. It is a humanitarian emergency unfolding in a region where communities' capacity to withstand another war has already been severely weakened. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Fragile healthcare system, deepening civilian suffering The resumption of hostilities in late September 2026 has intensified fears for civilians across Tigray. Reports from humanitarian organizations indicate that renewed fighting, drone strikes, and insecurity have placed civilians at greater risk while disrupting healthcare and other essential services. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) reported a sharp increase in war-wounded patients at hospitals in northern Ethiopia during the first days of renewed fighting. At facilities in Korem and Alamata, the number of wounded patients rose from approximately 180 over 48 hours to more than 420 between 22 and 25 September. Suhul Hospital in Shire also received more than 300 war-wounded patients by 25 September . These figures illustrate the immediate human cost of renewed hostilities and the pressure placed on an already fragile healthcare system. Medical teams must respond to growing emergency needs while insecurity restricts movement and makes it increasingly difficult to deliver assistance. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has also warned that renewed hostilities are heightening humanitarian concerns in northern Ethiopia. Although its teams have delivered medical supplies to health facilities across Tigray, continuing insecurity threatens civilians' access to treatment, food, clean water, electricity, and other necessities. For people who already face limited access to healthcare, renewed fighting presents an additional threat. Injured civilians may struggle to reach hospitals, while patients with chronic illnesses risk losing access to regular treatment. Disrupted electricity, shortages of medical supplies, and restrictions on movement can further undermine the ability of healthcare facilities to provide essential services. Protecting civilians must come before military objectives. Humanitarian access must come before political calculations." Behind every casualty figure is a person, a family, and a community facing uncertainty about survival. The growing pressure on hospitals is therefore not merely a question of medical capacity; it is a warning of the wider humanitarian consequences of renewed conflict. No safe place to return One of the most serious consequences of renewed fighting is the risk of further displacement. Thousands of families who have already experienced displacement may once again be forced to abandon their homes in search of safety. For many, however, leaving home does not guarantee protection. Displaced people may face shortages of food, shelter, clean water, medical care, and other essential supplies. The situation is particularly concerning for people displaced during the previous war who have been unable to return to their places of origin. Hundreds of thousands of people displaced from Western Tigray remain unable to return home, leaving families separated from their communities, land, property, and livelihoods. Renewed fighting threatens to compound their suffering by creating additional displacement while placing further pressure on the limited resources available to support existing displaced populations. The human cost of this prolonged displacement becomes clearer when the experiences of individual families are considered. In September 2026, I travelled to an internally displaced persons (IDP) centre in Mekelle as a research assistant, where I interviewed displaced families about their experiences and the hardships they continue to face. Among those I met was Senait Gebrekidan, who had been displaced from Humera, in Western Tigray. Senait described the dire living conditions facing displaced families, explaining that many were struggling to secure enough food to eat. According to her testimony, the 15-kilogram food ration that families were supposed to receive was frequently delayed. Essential items such as clothing, cooking oil, and medicine had become luxuries that many could no longer afford. She also reported that the last food distribution at the center had taken place in June, leaving families struggling to survive without regular assistance. Reports on IDP conditions in Tigray have repeatedly highlighted critical malnutrition and severe medicine shortages stemming from gaps in aid distribution. Her account illustrates how displacement can become a prolonged struggle for survival rather than a temporary escape from violence. For families such as Senait's, the absence of regular food assistance means that even the most necessities cannot be taken for granted. The hardship is especially severe for children, older people, pregnant women, people with disabilities, and individuals who require continuous medical treatment. Families forced to flee may lose access to education, healthcare, employment, and the social networks that once helped them cope with difficult circumstances. For displaced people, the crisis is not measured only by the distance they travel to escape violence. It is also measured by the length of time they remain without a safe home, adequate assistance, or a realistic prospect of rebuilding their lives. Senait's experience raises urgent questions about the adequacy and continuity of humanitarian assistance in displacement centers. When food distributions are delayed or interrupted, families already deprived of their homes and livelihoods are left with even fewer options for survival. Humanitarian organizations, government authorities, and international partners must ensure that displaced people receive regular assistance and adequate protection, regardless of where they originate or which areas they have been forced to leave. Fighting returns, hunger deepens Renewed fighting is unfolding amid an already severe food crisis. According to reporting on a September 2026 assessment by the Tigray Disaster Risk Management Commission, approximately 3.9 million people in the region require emergency food assistance . This situation has been aggravated by disrupted agricultural production, poor rainfall, inaccessible farmland, and the continuing consequences of years of conflict. Agriculture remains a principal source of livelihood for many households. Yet insecurity, displacement, damaged infrastructure, and limited access to farmland have undermined families' ability to produce sufficient food or earn an income. Renewed hostilities threaten to make matters worse by disrupting transportation, market activity, fuel supplies, and access to agricultural land. Farmers who cannot safely reach their fields may lose critical harvesting opportunities, while traders may struggle to transport food into affected communities. For displaced households, the consequences are particularly severe. Many have lost access to their land, livestock, and other productive assets. Without reliable humanitarian assistance or opportunities to earn an income, families may be unable to meet their basic nutritional needs. Senait's testimony provides a concrete example of this wider problem. The reported delays in food distributions at the Mekelle IDP center demonstrate how interruptions in assistance can leave already vulnerable families struggling to obtain even basic food supplies. The consequences extend beyond immediate hunger. Prolonged food shortages can lead to malnutrition, deteriorating health , interruptions to children's education, and the sale of essential household assets to survive. Children and people with existing health conditions are particularly vulnerable to the effects of inadequate nutrition. Humanitarian assistance must reach vulnerable communities before these pressures become even more severe. Regular emergency food distributions, nutrition programs, clean water, and healthcare support are essential to preventing further suffering. The reported food shortages in displacement centers also underscore the importance of monitoring humanitarian assistance to ensure that promised distributions are delivered consistently and that gaps are addressed before they become life-threatening. Humanitarian access under threat The ability of humanitarian organizations to respond effectively is another major concern. Insecurity can prevent aid workers from reaching affected communities, delay medical evacuations, interrupt the movement of relief supplies, and restrict the collection of reliable information about civilian needs. When fighting blocks humanitarian access , humanitarian agencies struggle to deliver food, medicine, and fuel where assistance is most urgently required. These obstacles are especially dangerous in a region where millions of people already depend on humanitarian support. The reported difficulties faced by displaced families illustrate why the continuity of humanitarian assistance is essential. When food distributions are interrupted, families who have lost their homes and livelihoods may have no alternative source of support. For those who depend on humanitarian aid for their daily survival, even a prolonged delay can have serious consequences. The international community must recognize that humanitarian access is not a secondary consideration to be addressed after military operations. It is an immediate necessity. All parties to the conflict must allow and facilitate rapid, safe, and unhindered humanitarian assistance to civilians in need. Humanitarian personnel, medical facilities, ambulances, relief convoys, and essential civilian infrastructure must be protected. The destruction, looting, or obstruction of facilities used to coordinate humanitarian assistance can have consequences far beyond the immediate damage. It can deprive entire communities of food, medicine, shelter, and other life-saving resources. Humanitarian organizations must also be able to assess needs independently and communicate their findings without intimidation or political interference. Beyond allowing aid to enter affected areas, humanitarian actors and relevant authorities must ensure that assistance reaches the people for whom it is intended. Displaced families need predictable, adequate, and continuous support, particularly where prolonged displacement has left them with few means of survival. Without safe access, reliable needs assessments, and sustained assistance, humanitarian organizations will struggle to respond to the growing demands of a population already weakened by years of conflict. From diplomatic statements to concrete action The international community cannot afford to treat renewed fighting in Tigray as another temporary security crisis. Years of violence have demonstrated the devastating consequences of delayed responses, inadequate civilian protection, and political agreements that fail to deliver lasting security. Statements expressing concern are important, but they are not enough. Civilians need practical measures that reduce the risk of further deaths, protect displaced families, and ensure that humanitarian assistance reaches those who need it. The United Nations, the African Union, the European Union, regional governments, and international humanitarian organizations should urgently coordinate efforts to implement the following measures. First, protect civilians . All parties must comply with international humanitarian law, distinguish between civilians and combatants, and take every feasible precaution to prevent civilian deaths and injuries. Attacks directed against civilians and civilian objects are prohibited. Second, secure humanitarian access . Safe and unhindered routes must be established for humanitarian convoys, medical teams, and emergency supplies. Communications and essential services should be restored wherever they have been disrupted. Third, expand emergency assistance . Food, clean water, shelter, medical supplies, and nutritional support must be prioritized for displaced people and communities facing acute shortages. Humanitarian partners should also assess the adequacy and regularity of food distributions in IDP centres to identify and address gaps in assistance. Fourth, strengthen independent monitoring . International and independent humanitarian and human rights organizations should have access to affected areas to assess civilian harm, investigate credible allegations of abuses, and document displacement and humanitarian needs. Fifth, protect displaced people's rights . Displaced families must not be forced to return to unsafe areas. Any return must be voluntary, safe, and dignified, with meaningful access to housing, land, property, essential services, and livelihoods. Sixth, intensify diplomatic efforts . Regional and international actors should press all parties to halt the escalation, return to a credible political process, and implement outstanding commitments under the Pretoria peace agreement. These measures should not depend on the political identity, ethnicity, or geographical location of the people affected. Humanitarian assistance must be provided according to need, and civilian protection must remain an obligation for all parties. International engagement must also extend beyond statements and emergency appeals. Diplomatic pressure, independent monitoring, and sustained engagement are necessary to prevent further escalation and ensure that commitments to peace translate into meaningful improvements in people's lives. Beyond emergency aid Emergency assistance can save lives, but it cannot independently resolve the underlying causes of the humanitarian crisis . A lasting solution requires more than temporary shelter and food distributions. It requires security, accountability, political dialogue, restored public services, and conditions that allow displaced people to rebuild their lives. The continued displacement of people from Western Tigray is a reminder that the consequences of the previous war remain unresolved. Sustainable solutions must address civilian protection, access to homes and property, and the rights of people who have been unable to return to their places of origin. For displaced families, a lasting solution means more than receiving food and shelter in temporary accommodation. It means having a realistic opportunity to return voluntarily to a safe environment, recover their livelihoods, reunite with their communities, and rebuild their lives with dignity. The people of Tigray should not have to endure another cycle of violence before the world responds with urgency." Until these conditions are established, many families will remain dependent on humanitarian assistance, exposed to insecurity, and uncertain about their future. The international community must also recognize that peace agreements cannot succeed through signatures alone. Their implementation must produce tangible improvements in the lives of ordinary people. The Pretoria agreement was intended to end a devastating war and create conditions for peace. Renewed fighting highlights the urgency of addressing outstanding political and security challenges through dialogue and implementation of the agreement's commitments. Without meaningful progress towards civilian protection, safe return, accountability, and political reconciliation, renewed fighting risks perpetuating a cycle in which each new escalation creates further displacement and deepens existing humanitarian needs. A sustainable response must therefore combine immediate humanitarian relief with long-term efforts to address insecurity, protect rights, restore essential services, and establish conditions for lasting peace. Conclusion: For Tigray's civilians, survival cannot wait Tigray stands at a dangerous crossroads. Renewed fighting threatens to deepen an already devastating humanitarian crisis, putting civilians at risk of death, displacement, hunger, and the loss of essential services. For families still struggling to recover from the previous war, another escalation represents not merely a political or military development but a renewed threat to their survival. The testimony of Senait Gebrekidan, a displaced woman from Humera whom I interviewed at an IDP centre in Mekelle, illustrates the daily hardships facing families who remain uprooted from their homes. Her account of delayed food distributions and the lack of access to essential items highlights the urgent need for reliable humanitarian assistance. Behind the wider figures on displacement and food insecurity are people trying to survive under conditions that no family should have to endure. Their suffering must not become normalized, and their needs must not be overlooked because the crisis has persisted for years. The international community must act before the situation deteriorates further. Humanitarian organizations need access, displaced families need protection, hospitals need supplies, and civilians need safety. The people of Tigray should not have to endure another cycle of violence before the world responds with urgency. Protecting civilians must come before military objectives. Humanitarian access must come before political calculations. And lasting peace must be measured by whether ordinary people can live safely in their homes, feed their families, access healthcare, and rebuild their futures. The time for urgent and coordinated humanitarian action is now. ethiopia.summary: Renewed fighting in Tigray, Ethiopia, threatens to exacerbate an already dire humanitarian crisis, nearly four years after the 2022 peace agreement aimed to end the conflict. The resurgence of hostilities has raised alarms about civilian safety, mass displacement, and food insecurity, with millions still grappling with the aftermath of previous violence. Reports indicate a sharp increase in war-related injuries, overwhelming an already fragile healthcare system. The International Committee of the Red Cross has warned that ongoing violence hampers access to essential services, including food and medical care. Displaced families, many unable to return home, face severe shortages of food, clean water, and shelter. Approximately 3.9 million people in Tigray require emergency food assistance, worsened by disrupted agricultural activities and insecurity. Humanitarian organizations emphasize the urgent need for consistent aid delivery and protection for civilians, highlighting that humanitarian access must take precedence over military objectives to prevent further suffering.

ethiopia.title: As Tens of Thousands Flee Ethiopia to Kenya, UN Agency Warns of Growing Humanitarian Needs
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: As Tens of Thousands Flee Ethiopia to Kenya, UN Agency Warns of Growing Humanitarian Needs - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: As Tens of Thousands Flee Ethiopia to Kenya, UN Agency Warns of Growing Humanitarian Needs Aquintero82/Wikimedia Commons A map showing the location of Kenya (in orange) and Ethiopia (in green). 30 October 2026 allAfrica.com By Peter Kenny Geneva — The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) says humanitarian needs are growing in an unfolding crisis on the Kenya–Ethiopia border as ongoing clashes on the Ethiopian side have forced tens of thousands of people to cross into Kenya in search of safety. Significant cross-border movements at Moyale have been reported since Oct. 22. “According to local authorities, up to an estimated 50,000 people have crossed into Kenya,” said Fatima Mohammed-Cole, the UNHCR Representative in Kenya. “The figure remains fluid as registration and verification efforts continue, amid reports of further crossings,” she said in a statement. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Many of those fleeing are women and children. The UN official said that while some affected people are staying with relatives and in host communities, others have sought shelter in temporary locations such as schools and churches. - FOOD: THE URGENT NEED “Food remains the most urgent need, alongside safe drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation and health care,” said Mohammed-Cole. UNHCR has deployed an emergency team to Moyale and is working closely with the Kenyan government. It is working alongside the UN migration agency, IOM; the UN children’s agency, UNICEF, the UN World Food Programme, the Kenya Red Cross Society, and other humanitarian partners, to support the national and local response. UNHCR said it is mobilising emergency relief supplies, including essential household items and temporary shelter materials, to support nearly 12,000 people, with efforts underway to increase assistance as needs grow. The agency is supporting ongoing assessments of protection and humanitarian needs. “We are also working with the authorities and partners to identify safer accommodation options, further away from the border, for those fleeing violence,” the UNHCR official said. According to Chatham House researchers, “Although Tigray has seen conflict before, this time there is a risk that hostilities could extend into Eritrea and Sudan,” they wrote . ethiopia.summary: The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) has reported a significant increase in humanitarian needs as tens of thousands flee Ethiopia to Kenya due to ongoing clashes. Since October 22, approximately 50,000 people have crossed the border at Moyale, with many being women and children. While some have found refuge with relatives or in host communities, others are sheltering in temporary locations like schools and churches. The most urgent needs identified include food, safe drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation, and healthcare. UNHCR has deployed an emergency team to assist and is collaborating with various humanitarian partners to provide essential supplies and support. Efforts are also underway to find safer accommodations for those fleeing violence. The situation remains fluid, with ongoing assessments of protection and humanitarian needs as the crisis unfolds.

ethiopia.title: PM Abiy Invites Russian Institutions to Partner With Ethiopia's AI University
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Invites Russian Institutions to Partner With Ethiopia's AI University - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Invites Russian Institutions to Partner With Ethiopia's AI University 29 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has called for deeper scientific cooperation with Russia, specifically inviting Russian institutions to partner with Ethiopia's newly established Medemer University of Artificial Intelligence. Addressing the 3rd Russia-Africa Summit, the Prime Minister emphasized the importance of building local technological capabilities. "Ethiopia is establishing the Medemer University of Artificial Intelligence in Addis Ababa. We invite Russian universities and institutions to work with us in teaching and research." Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The initiative is part of Ethiopia's broader push for "technological sovereignty," ensuring that AI development reflects local needs. "An African researcher should be able to create tools in the language of our people, and our institutions should decide how those tools use our data," he said. Beyond AI, PM Abiy identified food security and energy as key pillars for cooperation, including the development of a nuclear power plant to diversify Ethiopia's energy mix. He stressed that these partnerships must focus on tangible outcomes. "Innovation must find its way into production and trade", the Premier noted. Reflecting on the historical ties between the two nations, which date back to the late 19th century, he emphasized that modern cooperation must be backed by clear action plans. The PM concluded by highlighting that true independence requires both the right to decide and the ability to execute those decisions. "Independence gives us a right to decide. Capability gives us a means to put those decisions into action." Read the original article on ENA . Tagged: Ethiopia East Africa Governance Copyright © 2026 Ethiopian News Agency . ethiopia.summary: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has invited Russian institutions to collaborate with the newly established Medemer University of Artificial Intelligence in Addis Ababa. Speaking at the 3rd Russia-Africa Summit, he highlighted the need for enhanced scientific cooperation and local technological capabilities, emphasizing that AI development should cater to Ethiopian needs. Abiy stated, "An African researcher should be able to create tools in the language of our people," advocating for local control over data usage. He also identified food security and energy, including plans for a nuclear power plant, as key areas for partnership. The Prime Minister underscored the importance of actionable cooperation, asserting that innovation must translate into production and trade. Reflecting on the historical ties between Ethiopia and Russia, he called for modern collaborations to be supported by clear action plans, asserting that true independence involves both the right to make decisions and the capability to implement them.

ethiopia.title: Putin Hails Ethiopia-Russia Trade Surge to $1.3 Billion
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Putin Hails Ethiopia-Russia Trade Surge to $1.3 Billion - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Putin Hails Ethiopia-Russia Trade Surge to $1.3 Billion 29 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Russian President Vladimir Putin has hailed the sharp growth in bilateral trade between Russia and Ethiopia, which exceeded 1.3 billion USD in the first nine months of 2026. Putin underscored Moscow's commitment to deepening economic and trade cooperation with Ethiopia. "I would like to highlight the substantial growth in bilateral trade, which exceeded 1.3 billion USD in January-September this year. This is more than double the figure for the whole of 2025," he said. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Speaking during talks with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on the sidelines of the Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on October 28, Putin said trade between the two countries had more than doubled the total recorded for the whole of 2025. He described Ethiopia-Russia relations as friendly and constructive, highlighting promising opportunities for large-scale cooperation in energy, agriculture, industry, peaceful space exploration, science, healthcare and education. "We have many promising large-scale projects across a wide range of areas, from energy, agriculture and industrial cooperation to the peaceful exploration of outer space, science, healthcare and education," he said. Putin reaffirmed Russia's commitment to deepening its longstanding relations with Ethiopia. He also described bilateral ties and his personal contacts with PM Abiy as friendly, substantive and constructive. He recalled their recent meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi in September, where the two leaders reviewed key areas of bilateral cooperation, according to the Russian Foreign Ministry. The Russian President also emphasized the countries' coordination on international affairs through the United Nations, BRICS and other multilateral forums. He said Russia fully supports Africa's emergence as one of the key centres of the emerging multipolar world order. President Putin added that Moscow would pay particular attention to expanding trade and economic cooperation with African countries, ensuring food and energy security, and developing healthcare. He further wished Ethiopia success in hosting the 2027 United Nations Climate Change Conference in Addis Ababa. He noted that the Third Russia-Africa Summit would conclude with the adoption of a declaration and a new Action Plan of the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum covering 2027-2029. The meeting, he said, provided an opportunity to continue discussions on strengthening the multifaceted relations between Ethiopia and Russia, alongside current regional and international issues. ethiopia.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has praised the significant increase in trade between Russia and Ethiopia, which reached over $1.3 billion in the first nine months of 2026, more than doubling the total for 2025. During discussions with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed at the Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, Putin emphasized the importance of enhancing economic cooperation across various sectors, including energy, agriculture, industry, and healthcare. He described the relationship between the two nations as friendly and constructive, noting their collaboration in international forums like the UN and BRICS. Putin expressed support for Africa's role in the emerging multipolar world and highlighted Russia's commitment to food and energy security on the continent. He also wished Ethiopia success in hosting the 2027 United Nations Climate Change Conference. The summit is set to conclude with a new Action Plan for the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum covering the years 2027-2029. (160 words)
